stem: Which of these is a pasture legume?

options.content: Lucerne
Rhodes grass
Star grass
Kikuyu grass
options.rationale: A grass of cool, moist areas.

explanation: Lucerne is a legume; the others are grasses.

stem: Why are legumes included in a grass pasture?

options.content: They fix nitrogen and raise the protein in the feed
options.rationale: Correct: both animals and grass benefit.

options.content: They grow taller than the grass and shade out all weeds
They are never eaten, so they protect the soil
They make the soil more acid
options.rationale: Not a benefit; legumes prefer near-neutral soil.

explanation: Rhizobium in legume nodules fixes nitrogen, feeding the grass, and legumes are rich in protein.

stem: What is browse?

options.content: Dry grass cut and stored for winter
Leaves, shoots and pods of trees and shrubs
Green maize preserved in a pit
Short grass under trees

explanation: Browse is woody plant material eaten by livestock, especially goats.

stem: Why must pasture seed be sown into a fine, firm seedbed?

options.content: Fine soil holds more fertiliser than any other kind of soil
Firm soil keeps away all pests
The seeds are small and need close soil contact
options.rationale: Correct: they need moisture and shallow cover.

options.content: Large clods make the seed germinate too fast

explanation: Small seeds have little food store; they need firm contact with moist soil and shallow cover.

stem: When should a newly sown pasture first be grazed?

options.content: Heavily, as soon as the seedlings emerge
Lightly, once plants are firmly rooted
options.rationale: Correct: they are not pulled out.

options.content: Never: improved pastures are only cut for hay
Only after the plants have set seed and dried
options.rationale: Quality would be low and growth wasted.

explanation: Light, brief first grazing once plants are well rooted encourages tillering without uprooting.
hints: What happens if a weak seedling is tugged?

stem: Why is legume seed inoculated before sowing?

options.content: To kill weed seeds mixed with it
To make the seed heavier for broadcasting
To supply the right Rhizobium bacteria
options.rationale: Correct: for nodules and nitrogen fixation.

options.content: To protect the seed from birds

explanation: Inoculation coats the seed with the correct Rhizobium so nodules form and fix nitrogen.

stem: Cattle on veld in a high-rainfall area lose condition every dry season although grass is still standing. What best explains this?

options.content: It is sweet veld: the grass there is far too rich for cattle
options.rationale: Sweet veld keeps its value when dry.

options.content: Grass in high-rainfall areas has no fibre
The cattle are drinking too much water
It is sour veld: dry grass is low in quality

explanation: On sour veld (higher rainfall, leached soils) mature grass is low in protein and unpalatable, so animals need supplements in the dry season.
hints: Which kind of veld loses its value as it matures?

stem: Which pasture grass is usually established vegetatively from runners or splits?

options.content: Lucerne
Cowpea
Maize
options.rationale: A cereal crop, not a pasture grass.

options.content: Star grass

explanation: Star grass and Kikuyu are commonly planted from runners or root splits in moist soil.

stem: Browse is especially important for goats in the dry season because many tree leaves stay green and rich in protein.
explanation: True. Browse supplies protein after grasses have dried off.

stem: Match each establishment step with its reason.

right.content: Raises pH so legumes grow and nodulate
Firms soil around the small seeds

explanation: Each step solves a problem of young pasture.

stem: Complete the sentence.

payload.template: Legumes fix nitrogen with the help of {{blank:a}} bacteria living in swellings on their roots called {{blank:b}}.

explanation: *Rhizobium* in root nodules.

stem: Name the substance applied to an acid soil to raise its pH before sowing lucerne.
explanation: **Lime** (ground limestone).

stem: A field measures 180 m by 100 m. Assume grass seed is sown at 5 kg/ha. Calculate the mass of seed needed, in kg.
explanation: Area = 180 × 100 = 18,000 m² = 1.8 ha; 5 × 1.8 = 9 kg. Using m² instead of ha gives a huge figure.
workedSolution: 1. Area = 180 × 100 = 18,000 m² = 1.8 ha; 5 × 1.8 = 9 kg. Using m² instead of ha gives a huge figure.

stem: Single superphosphate is applied at 250 kg/ha to the same 1.8 ha field. How many 50 kg bags are needed? (Round UP to whole bags.)
A student counts seedlings in quadrats of 0.25 m² and finds a mean of 18 seedlings per quadrat. Calculate the number of seedlings per m².
explanation: 18 ÷ 0.25 = 72 seedlings per m². Multiplying by 0.25 gives 4.5.
workedSolution: 1. 18 ÷ 0.25 = 72 seedlings per m². Multiplying by 0.25 gives 4.5.
hints: How many 0.25 m² quadrats make 1 m²?

stem: A soil test recommends 2 t/ha of lime for a 1.8 ha field before lucerne is sown. Calculate the lime needed, in tonnes.
workedSolution:
1. Lime = rate × area.
2. 2 t/ha × 1.8 ha = 3.6 t.

stem: Describe **four** steps in preparing land and sowing an improved pasture.

points.description: Test the soil and lime if acid.
Clear, plough and harrow to a fine, firm seedbed.
Apply phosphorus fertiliser and sow certified seed (inoculated legumes) shallowly at the start of the rains.
Roll to firm the soil, then control weeds while the pasture establishes.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Test and lime the soil, plough and harrow to a fine firm seedbed, apply superphosphate and sow certified, inoculated seed shallowly at the start of the rains, and roll to firm the soil.

explanation: Soil, seedbed, sowing, after-care.
hints: From the soil to the seed.

stem: Suggest why a smallholder in a dry area might prefer to improve the management of natural veld rather than establish an improved pasture.

points.description: Establishing an improved pasture is costly (seed, fertiliser, lime, machinery, fencing).
In low, unreliable rainfall, sown species may fail or yield little without irrigation.
Better veld management (rotation, correct stocking, bush control) improves grazing at low cost and risk.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: An improved pasture needs seed, fertiliser, lime and machinery that a smallholder may not afford, and in a dry area it may fail without irrigation. Managing the veld better with correct stocking, rotation and bush control costs little and carries less risk.

explanation: Cost, climate and risk.
hints: Think of cost, rainfall and risk.

stem:
Students near Marondera sowed Rhodes grass on three plots with different seedbed treatments.

| Plot | Treatment | Seedlings per m² (four quadrats) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| P | Fine, firm seedbed; seed 1 cm deep; rolled | 64, 70, 58, 68 |
| Q | Fine seedbed; seed 1 cm deep; not rolled | 40, 46, 38, 44 |
| R | Cloddy seedbed; seed 5 cm deep; not rolled | 9, 12, 7, 8 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the mean number of seedlings per m² in plot P.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Express the mean for plot R as a percentage of the mean for plot P, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why plot P had more seedlings than plot Q.

points.description: Rolling firmed the soil around the seeds, giving close seed-soil contact.
Seeds took up water better / the surface did not dry out so quickly, so more germinated and established.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why so few seedlings established in plot R.

points.description: Pasture seeds are small with little stored food.
At 5 cm deep the seedlings used up their food before reaching the light and died.
Clods left air spaces so seeds had poor contact with moist soil.

explanation: Interpret an establishment trial and explain seedbed requirements.
hints: Think of seed size and depth.

stem:
Example results from three pastures on one farm.

| Pasture | Dry matter yield (t/ha) | Crude protein in dry matter (%) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Grass alone, no nitrogen | 4.2 | 7 |
| Grass alone + nitrogen fertiliser | 7.5 | 10 |
| Grass + legume mixture, no nitrogen | 6.8 | 14 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the crude protein produced per hectare by the grass-legume mixture, in kg/ha.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain why the mixture has the highest protein content although it received no nitrogen.

points.description: The legume fixes nitrogen from the air through Rhizobium in its nodules, some of which also reaches the grass.
Legume leaves are rich in protein, raising the protein of the mixture.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Suggest **two** advantages to a dairy farmer of the mixture over grass with nitrogen fertiliser.

points.description: Saves the cost of nitrogen fertiliser (and less risk of leaching).
More protein per hectare / higher-quality feed, so less protein concentrate is needed for milk.

explanation: Compare pastures by yield and protein.
hints: Protein (kg/ha) = DM yield in kg × CP % ÷ 100.
